messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Publisher
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

**Patient Name:** Samir
**Age:** 34
**Occupation:** Publisher
**Trauma:** Witnessing the violent assault of his younger brother

Samir is a carefully dressed man, his posture rigid, his eyes constantly scanning the room. He arrives for sessions directly from his office, the collar of his pressed shirt always buttoned to the top, a fortress of formality. He speaks in measured, deliberate sentences, as if editing his own thoughts before they can escape. He is a publisher, a man who curates stories for a living, but he cannot bear to tell his own.

The story begins eighteen months ago, on a Thursday evening. Samir’s younger brother, Karim, was leaving a small grocery store in their old neighborhood. Samir was waiting in the car, checking emails on his phone. He saw two men approach Karim. He remembers the casualness of it—a brief exchange, then a shove. Then the shove became a punch, and the punch became a rain of blows. Samir froze. His hand was on the door handle, but his body would not obey. He watched his brother fall, saw the sickening thud of a boot against his ribs, heard the wet, desperate sounds of a man being unmade. He did not get out of the car until the men were gone. By then, Karim was on the ground, bleeding from the mouth, his arm bent at an unnatural angle.

Samir drove him to the hospital. He remembers the red light he ran, the way his voice cracked when he screamed at the nurse. Karim survived. He has a metal plate in his arm and a slight limp, but he is alive. Samir, however, did not survive the same way.

In the months since, Samir has become a ghost in his own life. At work, his precision has turned to paralysis. He was once known for championing debut authors, for taking risks on difficult, raw narratives. Now, every manuscript feels like a threat. He finds himself rejecting stories of violence, of urban crime, of family conflict. He cannot read a scene with a physical altercation without his heart hammering against his ribs. He recently killed a beloved series by a bestselling author because the protagonist was a detective. “Too gritty,” he told the author. The real reason, he cannot say, is that the word “detective” makes him see the police report, the clinical language used to describe his brother’s broken body.

At home, he is a stranger to his wife, Nadia. He cannot sleep beside her. He lies on the floor of the nursery they have yet to use, the one they were painting the week of the attack. He sleeps in short, panicked bursts, waking with a jolt, convinced he hears the sound of boots on pavement. He has not been back to that street. He takes three different routes to work, rotating them so no one can predict his path. He checks the back seat of his car every time before he gets in, a ritual he knows is irrational but cannot stop.

The worst part is the guilt. It is a physical weight in his chest. He replays the scene in a loop, editing it, rewriting it. In his head, he gets out of the car. He yells. He fights. In reality, he was a spectator to his own brother’s destruction. He feels he failed the most basic test of brotherhood. He no longer looks Karim in the eye. He sends money, but he cannot visit. He cannot bear to see the limp, the reminder of his own cowardice.

Last week, a junior editor dropped a heavy stack of paper on his desk. The sound was a gunshot. Samir dove under his desk, his hands over his head, his breath ragged. He stayed there for ten minutes, trembling, while his assistant called his wife. He told HR he had vertigo. But when he looks in the mirror, he sees a man who is not brave, who is not safe, who is still sitting in that car, watching his brother fall.
